The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

According to recent reports, the 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

It has been revealed that batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

Recent findings suggest that the decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the crucial thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

In a recent development, talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Recent findings suggest that pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

It has been revealed that your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

According to recent reports, once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

Industry observers note that the most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and organization handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Sources indicate that report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Sources indicate that start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

According to recent reports, dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP swiftly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

#68902. The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1878 w)
📖 Baca

The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Industry observers note that designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach. He loves speaking at conferences like Smashing Conf and is a founding member of the Adobe Design … More about Andy ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way. Not always in those exact words, obviously. It usually comes out as something more reasonable: we didn’t get enough engineering time, product had already decided the solution, the roadmap was too packed, leadership only cared about this quarter’s numbers, research got cut, the experiment was never run properly, the design debt was known about, but nobody wanted to spend a sprint fixing it.

According to recent reports, much of this is true. Most designers have worked inside that awkward middle space between product and engineering. Product frames the problem, or at least thinks it does. Engineering decides what is feasible, or at least what is affordable. Design is expected to make the thing clearer, simpler, more coherent, more usable, and occasionally more desirable, while also being careful not to disrupt the plan too much.

That position has always been uncomfortable.

They can spot the broken onboarding flow, the confusing upgrade path, the empty state that makes owners feel stupid, the feature that looks reasonable in a product review but makes no sense in real use. Seeing the problem is one thing. Getting it fixed is another.

So design often becomes an argument. You make the case. You annotate the flow. You bring the research clip. You point to the support tickets. You show the Figma prototype. You explain why the “small edge case” is actually the first-run experience for half your latest users. Then everyone nods, agrees it matters, and moves on to whatever had already made it onto the roadmap.

It has been revealed that this is one reason AI is more interesting for design than the usual “will it replace designers?” debate suggests. The real change is not that designers can make more screens. Nobody needs more screens. The interesting change is that designers may need less permission.

A good designer can now move from “we should fix this” to “I fixed this, and pushed it live.” They can prototype the alternative onboarding flow, write and test clearer product copy, build a rough working version of the interaction, clean up small pieces of design debt without waiting three months for a roadmap slot, and make the better thing visible enough that it becomes harder to ignore.

That changes the politics of the work. Design has often relied on persuasion because designers lacked direct means of production. AI weakens that dependency. Not everywhere, and not for everything. Complex products still have architecture, infrastructure, data models, permissions, security, compliance, legacy systems, and all the other unglamorous reasons software is hard. But the boundary is moving.

In this version of the future, designers become less permission-dependent: less reliant on product to bless the problem, less reliant on engineering to make every small improvement real, less trapped in the role of internal critic, taste-provider, or Figma operator. More able to make, test, repair, and ship.

The best designers start to look less like traditional product designers and more like hybrid product leaders. They still care about interaction, hierarchy, language, flow, brand and craft, but they also understand the commercial shape of the problem. They can make trade-offs. They can prototype in code, or close enough to code. They can use AI to explore options rapidly, then use judgment to throw most of them away. They can sit with a founder or PM and move from a vague product concern to something tangible by the end of the day.

In a recent development, there may be fewer of these people, but they will be harder to ignore. The current design-org model was partly built around scarcity: scarce engineering time, slow production, expensive prototypes, handoffs between specialists, heavy coordination across teams. If AI reduces some of that scarcity, it probably reduces the need for some of the roles that grew around it. The optimistic case is not that every designer keeps their job and gets a productivity boost. That feels like wishful thinking. The more believable version is that the total number of designers goes down, but the designers who remain have more direct influence over the product.

It has been revealed that that is not a bad outcome for the strongest designers. It may even be the thing many of them have wanted for years.

Autonomy has teeth. If AI gives designers more room to act, it also removes some of the cover. The same constraints that held good designers back have also protected weaker ones from being tested too directly.

According to recent reports, for years, it has been easy to say: I had a better idea, but we never got the engineering time. Sometimes that was exactly what happened. Sometimes the better idea was never really more than a critique. It had not been made concrete. It had not been tested. It had not dealt with the awkward trade-offs. It sounded strong because it lived safely in opposition to the shipped thing.

According to recent reports, if you can prototype the recommendation, the recommendation has to get better. If you can make the alternative flow, the flow has to survive contact with details. If you can test the product copy, you have to care what happens when people read it. If you can fix the small piece of design debt, you have to decide whether it was really worth fixing.

In a recent development, some designers are not as strategic as they think they are. They have learned the language of strategy without the discomfort of owning outcomes. They can talk about user needs, business goals, systems thinking, and product quality, but struggle when asked to make a call. They want influence, but not the exposure that comes with it.

Sources indicate that the profession has spent a long time arguing that design deserves more power. Fine. But more power means fewer excuses. It means the work is judged less by the elegance of the argument and more by the quality of the thing you made, tested, or changed. That is a better standard, but it will not be kind to everyone.

There is a second bear case, and it is probably the one large design teams should worry about most. Product and engineering already have more institutional power than design in most companies. They own the roadmap, the technical architecture, the sprint machinery, the metrics, and usually the language leadership understands. Design often has to translate its concerns into someone else’s terms before they count.

In a recent development, AI may not rebalance that power. It may hand product and engineering enough design capability to make design easier to bypass. A PM who can generate a decent flow, decent copy, and a decent prototype may not feel the same need to involve design early. An engineer who can use AI to produce a reasonable interface may decide the design system covers enough of the decision-making. A founder who can get to a polished demo in an afternoon may confuse polish with product thinking.

It has been revealed that the problem is not that these people will suddenly become great designers. The problem is that many companies do not know the difference between great design and plausible design. Plausible design is dangerous. It looks coherent in a product review. It uses the right components. The spacing is fine. The copy is not embarrassing. The flow mostly works. Nobody in the meeting feels strongly enough to object. So it ships.

If a manufacturer already thinks design is mostly screens, prototypes, and polish, AI gives it a cheaper way to get those things.

In a recent development, in that world, design does not gain more agency. It gets narrowed. The remaining designers manage the design system, police component usage, review flows that have already been decided, tidy the interface, maintain brand consistency, and get pulled into high-stakes introduces, executive demos, and the occasional messy cross-platform problem. Useful work, but a smaller surface area. Less shaping the product, more maintaining the furniture.

This is why the “AI will automate the boring 20%” argument feels too comforting. In some companies, perhaps that is what happens. But in large tech organisations, where design teams grew around coordination, production and process, the cut could be much deeper. Not 20%. Maybe 50%. Maybe more. Especially in places where leadership never really understood why the design team had grown so large in the first place.

The painful part is that both futures can be true at the same time. AI can make the best designers more capable and many average designers less necessary. It can give design more agency while reducing design headcount. It can help a small number of designers move closer to product leadership while pushing others into governance and clean-up work. It can free designers from waiting for permission, then reveal that some were more comfortable waiting than acting.

The designers who do well will not be the ones who merely use AI to produce more options. Options are cheap now. They will be the ones who know which option is worth pursuing, why it matters, how to test it, what to cut, where the product is lying to itself, and when “good enough” is quietly damaging the business.

They will have taste, but taste will not be enough. They will need product judgment, technical curiosity, commercial awareness and the nerve to make decisions before every variable is settled. They will need to be comfortable moving between a customer conversation, a prototype, a pricing concern, a brand question, and a messy implementation detail without insisting that all of those belong to someone else.

I’m not completely sure where we end up. I hope it is closer to the bull case: fewer permission structures, more making, more agency, better designers finally able to show what they can do without being held back by the machinery around them.

I fear it may be closer to the bear case: product and engineering absorb much of the work, companies decide plausible design is good enough, and design loses status, headcount, and strategic ground.

In reality, it will probably be some uncomfortable mix of the two. Some designers will use AI to gain more agency. Some companies will use it to need fewer designers. Some teams will produce better work because the distance between judgment and execution gets shorter. Others will ship more plausible mediocrity because nobody in the room can tell the difference.

For years, designers have stated they could create more value if they were less constrained by the organisation around them. AI is about to test that claim. Some will finally get to prove it. Some will find out the constraints were doing them a favour.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.

“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” claims the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”.

Simone Crestani’s Forsythia (2026), on show with Lebanese art and design gallery PIK’D at Nomad Abu Dhabi Courtesy PIK’D and NOMAD Abu Dhabi 2026.

This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.

Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.

Industry observers note that bellavance‑Lecompte indicates that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.

Another key development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something upcoming can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte states.

Sources indicate that for Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte says. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year highlighted us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.

• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November.

#68897. Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1545 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.
  • In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory.
  • The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027.

In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.

The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.

Emirati artist Shaikha Al Mazrou at the Cultural Foundation, where she is staging a solo show Courtesy the Cultural Foundation.

Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027.

Sources indicate that in 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.

She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside latest commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.

Recent findings suggest that installation view: All Manner of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, 2026. Pictured here: Rand Abdul Jabbar, Earthly Wonders, Celestial Beings (series), (2024).

NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027.

Sources indicate that in 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Said established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.

All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.

Industry observers note that the exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Noted’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.

In a recent development, A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.

A carved ivory jewelled casket on show in the exhibition Spices and Wonders at Louvre Abu Dhabi © Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi; Photo: Sylvie Van Roey.

Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027.

The Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.

This investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).

Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.

Luisa Dörr, various works from Escaramuzas, (2024–ongoing).

Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November.

The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.

Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.

The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu shows life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.

Courtesy of the artist and ATHR Gallery.

The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.

One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.

Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.

Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.

Fresh Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.

Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.

Installation view of Rohini Devasher, Latent Fields (Field Five) (2023); Latent Fields (Field Six) (2023).

Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December.

The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.

In a recent development, in Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.

The work—a fresh iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—reveals how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.

Devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.

In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

#68896. How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3055 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

In a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

The reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

Industry observers note that in this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

Sources indicate that before we start deleting things, let’s quickly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

According to recent reports, baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:.

That 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

You can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page shows a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

It’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your consumers, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

So before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

Industry observers note that not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your users would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

It has been revealed that 2. What does the swap actually cost?

According to recent reports, dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

Recent findings suggest that libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

It has been revealed that keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

Industry observers note that this is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:.

Let’s walk through some of them.

It has been revealed that timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

The numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

You may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:.

Sources indicate that humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:.

Recent findings suggest that one thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

If your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

The browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

In a recent development, the one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():.

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:.

It has been revealed that I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of owners and have seen lots of success with it.

None of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

It has been revealed that the libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

Calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

That single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:.

It has been revealed that clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

Industry observers note that the other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:.

Industry observers note that anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between , the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

Lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:.

According to recent reports, there’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

In a recent development, lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:.

Sources indicate that structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:.

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Sources indicate that not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it indicates the framework telling you to wait.

Temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

It has been revealed that however, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari consumers don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

According to recent reports, the official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

Sources indicate that the verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for users on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

It has been revealed that the clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to customers:.

Industry observers note that for a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

For each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

In a recent development, for each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

For Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the new code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:.

That way you ship less code to the consumers who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

Industry observers note that add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.).

I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:.

Industry observers note that none of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships upcoming features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

Similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser claims.

Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser states.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

With over 14 years of experience and deep expertise in API development, third-party tool integration, and scalable software solutions, Alexey specializes in … More about Alexey ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Isadora Agency who help enterprise brands and market leaders navigate digital, evolve profitably, and launch unforgettable websites, products, and campaigns. Thank you!

Recent findings suggest that when front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

When our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

Sources indicate that we didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Recent findings suggest that our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

It has been revealed that for instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

Sources indicate that the tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

Because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

To achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:.

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:.

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:.

According to recent reports, the result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

Industry observers note that because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Industry observers note that since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:.

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:.

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:.

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:.

Sources indicate that another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

In a recent development, we handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:.

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

Lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:.

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

Because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

It has been revealed that compound interest is often called the eighth wonder of the world, and for good reason. It is the mathematical force that turns consistent, modest investing into life-changing wealth — and it is the foundation of every financial independence plan.

Sources indicate that here is the core concept. Simple interest earns a return only on your original deposit. If you invest $10,000 at 7% simple interest, you earn $700 per year — every year, forever, on the same $10,000 base. After 30 years, you would have $31,000.

Compound interest earns a return on your original deposit plus all the interest previously earned. In Year 1, you earn $700 on your $10,000. In Year 2, you earn 7% on $10,700 — that is $749. In Year 3, you earn 7% on $11,449 — that is $801. Each year, your interest earns its own interest, and the growth accelerates.

After 30 years of compound interest at 7%, your $10,000 grows to approximately $76,123 — more than double the $31,000 from simple interest. And that is with a single $10,000 deposit and no additional contributions.

The difference starts small and then explodes. In the first 10 years, compound interest adds only $2,672 more than simple interest. In the last 10 years (year 20 to 30), it adds over $30,000 more. This accelerating curve is why time in the market matters more than almost any other factor in building wealth.

According to recent reports, investing $500 per month at a 7% average annual return — roughly the inflation-adjusted historical return of the S&P 500 — produces dramatically different results depending on how long you invest. After 10 years: $86,500. After 20 years: $260,500. After 30 years: $567,000. You contribute $180,000 of your own money over 30 years. Compound interest adds $387,000 — more than double your contributions. Time is the multiplier that no amount of additional savings can replace.

The compound interest formula is straightforward once you understand the components:.

For a $10,000 investment at 7% compounded monthly for 30 years:.

A = 10,000 x (1 + 0.07/12)^(12 x 30) = 10,000 x (1.00583)^360 = $81,165.

Notice this is higher than the $76,123 from annual compounding — more frequent compounding produces slightly more growth, though the difference is modest.

The jump from annual to monthly compounding is meaningful. The jump from monthly to daily is negligible. Most bank accounts and investment returns compound daily or monthly, so you are already getting nearly the maximum benefit.

Recent findings suggest that the Rule of 72 is the single most useful mental math shortcut in personal finance. Divide 72 by your expected annual return to estimate how many years it takes to double your money.

At a 7% real return, your money doubles every 10 years. A $100,000 portfolio at age 25 becomes $200,000 at 35, $400,000 at 45, and $800,000 at 55 — even with zero additional contributions. This is why starting early is the single most powerful financial decision you can make.

It has been revealed that the following table highlights how different monthly contribution amounts grow over time at a 7% average annual return (roughly the inflation-adjusted long-term return of the US stock market). These numbers assume you start with $0 and contribute consistently every month.

According to recent reports, notice the pattern: the growth in the third decade dwarfs the first two decades combined. At $1,000 per month, you accumulate $173,000 in the first 10 years but $613,000 in the last 10 years — with the same monthly contribution. This is compound interest in its most powerful phase.

The 7% figure used above is already adjusted for historical inflation (the nominal S&P 500 return has averaged roughly 10%, minus approximately 3% average inflation). This means the projections above represent real purchasing power — $567,000 in 30 years would buy roughly what $567,000 buys today.

If you use a nominal return of 10% instead, the numbers look even more dramatic, but they overstate your future purchasing power. Always use inflation-adjusted returns (6-7%) for retirement planning and real purchasing power comparisons.

According to recent reports, consider two investors. Investor A starts investing $500 per month at age 25 and stops at age 35 — investing for only 10 years, then letting it grow untouched until age 65. Investor B waits until age 35 and invests $500 per month every month from 35 to 65 — investing for 30 years.

Industry observers note that investor A contributes one-third the money and ends up with more at 65. The 10-year head start gave compound interest enough time to overcome the difference. This is not a trick — it is the fundamental math of compounding. Every year you delay costs you more than the money you eventually invest.

Put the math to work starting today.

Recent findings suggest that the single most important factor in compound interest is time, not amount. Even $100 per month started today beats $500 per month started five years from now over a long enough timeline. Open a brokerage account or increase your 401(k) contribution today.

Pro tip: Automate your contributions so they happen before you see the money in your checking account.

The historical 7-10% average return comes from broad stock market index funds. A total US stock market fund or S&P 500 fund with an expense ratio below 0.10% gives you the full benefit of compound growth without high fees eroding your returns.

Recent findings suggest that when you get a raise, increase your monthly investment by at least half the raise amount. This prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming your additional income and accelerates compound growth.

Pro tip: A 3% annual raise invested means your contributions grow exponentially alongside your investment returns.

Set all your accounts to automatically reinvest dividends. Dividend reinvestment is compound interest within compound interest — your dividends buy more shares, which generate more dividends, which buy more shares.

Market downturns are not a reason to sell — they are the cost of admission for long-term compound growth. Every major market crash in history has been followed by recovery and new highs. Pulling money out during a downturn and reinvesting later is the most reliable way to destroy compound interest.

Pro tip: If seeing your balance drop causes panic, check your portfolio less frequently. Quarterly or annually is enough.

Simple interest is calculated only on your original principal. Compound interest is calculated on your principal plus all previously earned interest. Over long periods, the difference is enormous — $10,000 at 7% for 30 years grows to $31,000 with simple interest but $76,123 with compound interest.

Industry observers note that more frequent compounding produces slightly higher returns, but the difference is small. Monthly compounding at 7% on $10,000 for 30 years yields $81,165 versus $76,123 for annual compounding — a difference of about 6.6%. Most investment accounts compound daily or when dividends are reinvested, so you are already receiving near-optimal compounding.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Compound interest (more accurately, compound growth) applies to any investment account where your returns are reinvested. In a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account invested in index funds, your gains generate additional gains. Tax-advantaged accounts like Roth IRAs are especially powerful because the compounding occurs entirely tax-free.

Recent findings suggest that the S&P 500 has returned approximately 10% annually in nominal terms over the past century. Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7%. For conservative planning, use 6-7% to account for inflation. For nominal calculations (not inflation-adjusted), use 9-10%. Using rates above 10% for long-term projections is overly optimistic for a diversified portfolio.

Yes — and the math is surprisingly accessible. Investing $1,000 per month at a 7% real return reaches $1,134,000 in 30 years (you contribute $360,000, compound interest adds $774,000). At $500 per month, you reach $567,000 in 30 years. The key variables are consistent contribution, a reasonable return, and patience.

Compound interest is the mathematical engine behind financial independence. The FI community uses compound growth to accumulate 25x their annual expenses in invested assets (the 4% rule). By saving 50%+ of income and investing in index funds that compound at 7-10% annually, FIRE practitioners can reach financial independence in 10-17 years rather than the traditional 40-year career.

Compound interest is the most powerful wealth-building force available to ordinary investors. The math is unambiguous: $500 per month at 7% becomes $567,000 in 30 years, with compound interest contributing more than twice what you personally invest. The two factors you control — how much you invest and how long you stay invested — matter far more than picking the "right" stocks or timing the market. Start today, invest in low-cost index funds, reinvest all dividends, and do not interrupt the compounding. Time is your greatest asset, and every year you wait costs more than you think.

Giant comets blaze across dark skies, volcanoes rain down fire on hapless cities, floods rage and the moon turns blood red in a spectacular 16th-century manuscript coming up for auction at Christie’s in London, estimated between £700,000 and £1m.

The Book of Miracles, with 167 vivid watercolours illustrating natural phenomena—real and imagined—and scenes from the Old and Fresh Testaments, was completed in Augsburg, Germany, around 1552. It is attributed to Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, painters, print makers and designers who had separate workshops but sometimes collaborated on notable commissions.

According to recent reports, A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

Industry observers note that eugenio Donadoni, the director and international specialist in Medieval and Renaissance manuscripts at Christie’s, called the book an exquisite work, with its illustrations as vibrant after nearly 500 years as the day they were made. “Beyond their extraordinary beauty, these images offer us a glimpse into how people in the 16th century made sense of a world that could often seem mysterious and unpredictable. Today, we might understand a comet, an eclipse or an earthquake through science, but in the Renaissance these phenomena could be interpreted as signs of something greater, even as warnings of what was to come,” he says. “The manuscript brings together the remarkable visual imagination of the period, the events that captured people's attention and provoked their wonder and fear. Nearly 500 years later, these images remain as compelling as ever.”.

Industry observers note that A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

The book is included in a series of sales of works from the Mickey Cartin collection. Cartin, who is based in Connecticut and built the electrical supply firm founded by his grandfather into a national firm, began collecting in the 1980s across many categories, including books and manuscripts, old master paintings, furniture and contemporary art. Artnews included in him in its Top 200 Collectors list every year from 2007-13. He bought The Book of Miracles in 2010, three years after it was rediscovered in a private collection in Bavaria, and it acquired wider fame when the art publisher Taschen published a facsimile edition in 2013.

The manuscript, part of the sale An Alchemy of Ideas: Works from the Mickey Cartin Collection, will be on public view at Christie’s King Street sales room in London on 4-10 December, before the sale on 10 December.

Breaking: New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling
