💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers.
  • Industry observers note that “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon.
  • According to recent reports, tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Nike.

Sportswear brand Nike has unveiled the 3D-printed air bags that will be used for its next generation of air-filled trainers. In this interview, the brand’s chief innovation, design & product officer Phil McCartney explains why it is a technological and performance advance.

Industry observers note that “I see it personally as a revolution, not an evolution,” McCartney told Dezeen from the LeBron James Innovation Center in Oregon. “It’s a huge stride forward.”.

According to recent reports, tuned Air was designed to give Nike much greater control of how air is used within the midsole to provide cushioning and support. Using a combination of proprietary 3D printing and “selective lamination” allows Nike to create midsoles that perform in different ways under different parts of the foot.

Informed by the raised vibrant colours on magazine covers, the airbag is built up from layers of ink.

“We can engineer the structure and tune the structure in the heel differently to the forefoot,” mentioned McCartney.

“We can also tune the height, so you can have a variety of different heights, and we can tune the structure inside.”.

Nike unveiled the technology and concept images for a running shoe today, and is planning for the first Nike Tuned Air trainer to be launched next year.

The trainers will be the first in what Nike sees as a third major generation of its air-filled shoes, since Nike CEO Phil Knight worked with inventor Frank Rudy to use a cushioning system filled with gas in the late 1970s.

Following the Nike Air Tailwind in 1978, Nike developed Air Max in the 1980s and Air Zoom in the 1990s.

Sources indicate that “At its core, Air, for 50 years, has been this magical combination of lightweight, cushioned and resilient – it doesn’t break down over time,” mentioned McCartney. “That’s why from day one when Phil [Knight] struck the deal with Frank Rudy, we’ve been so committed to it – it just delivers a really unique benefit.”.

Sources indicate that “If Max Air is about maximal cushioning and impact protection, Zoom Air is more about responsiveness and snappiness,” he continued. “Tuned Air, because of this proprietary ink and selective lamination process, allows us to literally tune the sensation within the airbag, which enables us to sort of move free from the constraints of typical geometry and shape.”.

According to McCartney, this change in how the airbags are manufactured opens up possibilities, especially in customisation.

It has been revealed that “It is the first step in exploring all the different places that this will go,” noted McCartney. “The capability and what we’re able to do with this proprietary ink and the selective lamination allows us to really unlock the real potential of air.”.

“It also creates this canvas for all the design explorations that we’ve always wanted to do, but the limitations of the manufacturing process didn’t allow,” he continued.

Sources indicate that “So now the handcuffs are off in terms of it being a canvas – what expressions do we want to explore? What different visuals, geometries, and different ways to articulate the benefit can we explore? We’re looking at all of that. “.

While the air-filled midsole has been manufactured, the trainer is still in development. However, McCartney expects the shoe to look close to the concept render that was revealed today.

“There’ll be a few modifications,” he remarked. “Knowing where the design is going to go. It’s pretty representative as an illustration, but it isn’t the final design.” He noted that the final air bag design will be close to the prototype.

“What we’re exploring now is how do we take the idea of lightweight cushioning and this idea of tuned [and find] what that looks like in an expression and an experience on the upper.”.

One key design element that will feature in the commercial release next year will be the full-length, visible air bag, which McCartney said is an “key part of the design and important part of this platform”.

The midsoles are the latest innovation in Nike’s exploration of using air within footwear and apparel. While it has made millions of shoes containing air, it has also recently unveiled the inflating Air Milano Jacket at 2026 Winter Olympics and its Radical AirFlow t-shirts that counterintuitively use more material to make a wearer cooler.

In all the areas of innovation that McCartney oversees at Nike, air is where he sees the most potential.

Industry observers note that “There’s a number of areas, but if I had to pick one, I think that [air] is the platform that intrigues us most, that drives our creativity the most, that also translates into the biggest athlete benefit. And I mean athlete in the broadest sense of the term – if you’ve got a body, you’re an athlete.”.

“We’re really intrigued and fascinated by the notion of being able to harness what’s all around us to further performance,” mentioned McCartney. “That started in footwear, obviously. This is the next revolution.”.

Photography courtesy of Nike.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sotheby’s today declared that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in Fresh York.

In a recent development, the Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

Sources indicate that the Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”.

Recent findings suggest that the provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Recent findings suggest that last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he indicates took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a latest generation of collectors.”.

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this month, Trump’s White House ballroom and military bunker laid its final structural steel beam, with politicians and critics weighing in on the scale of the project.

Recently taken images of the extension, which show the structure with massive concrete shear walls, steel beams, and columns, along with a partially enclosed roof structure, have drawn attention to the scale of the building.

No sign of its planned neoclassical ornamentation has yet been implemented.

Officially called the East Wing Modernization Project, the structure dwarfs the Executive Residence and West Wing.

Trump confirmed the laying of the last steel beam in the superstructure on 4 November, the day after the national midterm elections.

“This is a special structure,” Trump said on a tour on 4 November, according to NBC News. “It’s going to be not only one of the biggest, but it’ll be the most beautiful ballroom, I think, anywhere in the world, and they’ve been trying to get it for 150 years.”.

It indicates everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People's House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/ou23LpAes8.

Since then, there has been a renewed wave of criticism online over the project, ranging from outrage to humour.

Former senator and presidential candidate Hillary Clinton wrote on X (formerly Twitter), commenting on the size of the structure and noting the midterm election’s “repudiation” of Trump.

“It says everything about Donald Trump that his gilded ballroom dwarfs the size of the People’s House—and it says everything about the American people that they repudiated him loudly and clearly last Tuesday,” wrote Clinton.

Congressman Jim Clyburn took a similar stance in a statement on Facebook, noting that the ballroom was “much bigger” than the rest of the White House.

Architecture critic Kate Wagner took a more humorous approach, noting that the ballroom is not neoclassical in construction. Wagner compared it to a Ramada Inn, a chain of hotels in the US, that they will “glue pediments to”.

“[It’s] an outcome designed in a lab to make everyone angry. possibly the most trump building ever built,” wrote Wagner on X.com.

The ballroom has been controversial since Trump demolished the White House’s East Wing in October 2025. The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project in April.

It has faced legal challenges, with US District Judge Leon issuing a stay in response to a lawsuit led by the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

the fact that trump's ballroom is clearly not neoclassical in any way shape or form is possibly the funniest moment in architectural history.

In August, the Supreme Court allowed the project to continue, though the dissenting opinion stated it was “likely unlawful”.

Despite the legal challenges, construction has continued, with Trump’s team leaning on the national security aspects of the underground bunker.

Sources indicate that the administration has also floated plans to add a screening facility at Sherman Park – a small park to the southwest of the White House. Trump also installed a paved helipad on the White House lawn.

  • The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.
  • The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.
  • Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” mentioned the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

“What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges said. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

It has been revealed that “The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

First, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

In a recent development, “Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

Recent findings suggest that baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes customers away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” stated the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges said.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic manufacturer, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” said the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges mentioned “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

Sources indicate that “Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they noted. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” remarked the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart latest vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart new vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

Sources indicate that “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

“This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges mentioned. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

“This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges stated. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

Recent findings suggest that “This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” said the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

Industry observers note that “As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.
  • The mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point.
  • The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

The mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

The identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron says the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert upcoming audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz says the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • According to recent reports, the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

In a recent development, the repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

According to recent reports, the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

Sources indicate that “This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, remarked during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

According to recent reports, brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she stated. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

Recent findings suggest that A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

It has been revealed that more than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

It has been revealed that the good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:.

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits.

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS states "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Recent findings suggest that let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 1: Calculate Combined Income.

It has been revealed that step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

According to recent reports, step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:.

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:.

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

It has been revealed that this is the single most powerful strategy. Roth IRA withdrawals are not included in the combined income formula. If you retire early (before Social Security age), you have a window of low-income years to convert Traditional IRA/401(k) money to Roth.

Example: Between ages 55 and 67, you convert $500,000 from your Traditional IRA to a Roth — paying tax at rates as low as 10-12%. When you claim Social Security at 67, your Roth withdrawals don't push you into a higher SS taxation tier. Instead of 85% of your benefits being taxable, you might pay tax on 0-50%.

Sources indicate that the math is dramatic over a 25+ year retirement. Converting at 12% during early retirement to avoid 22%+ taxation on Social Security for decades produces enormous tax savings.

Sources indicate that every dollar of AGI pushes you toward the 50% or 85% taxation tiers. Strategic levers include:.

In a recent development, once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. This satisfies your Required Minimum Distribution (RMD) without the distribution being included in your AGI. Lower AGI means lower combined income, which means less Social Security is taxable.

For charitably inclined retirees, QCDs are one of the most tax-efficient giving strategies available — they simultaneously reduce your income tax AND reduce the tax on your Social Security benefits.

Recent findings suggest that delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 increases your benefit by roughly 77%. But there's a secondary benefit: during the delay years, you have more room to do Roth conversions at low tax rates without Social Security benefits adding to your combined income. The combination of larger benefits and lower taxation on those benefits makes delay doubly powerful for tax optimization.

If you retire before claiming Social Security, you have a golden window for Roth conversions. With little or no earned income and no SS benefits, you can convert Traditional IRA money to Roth at the lowest tax brackets of your lifetime. Every dollar you convert is a dollar that will never increase the tax on your Social Security benefits. This window closes permanently once you start claiming.

A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

Sources indicate that list your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

Compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

For the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

The taxable portion of your Social Security gets added to your other taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. Check if your state also taxes Social Security.

Sources indicate that for single filers, Social Security becomes partially taxable when combined income exceeds $25,000 (50% tier) and up to 85% taxable above $34,000. For married filing jointly, the thresholds are $32,000 (50% tier) and $44,000 (85% tier). These thresholds have not changed since 1993 and are not indexed for inflation.

This distinction matters for things like the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), IRA contribution eligibility, and the Social Security earnings test (which only applies to earned income like wages and self-employment).

Sources indicate that social Security benefits are included in the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) calculation that determines Medicare Part B and Part D premium surcharges (IRMAA). High-income retirees can pay significantly more for Medicare — up to 3.4 times the standard premium. Managing MAGI in retirement affects both Social Security taxation and Medicare costs.

There have been numerous proposals to reform Social Security taxation, including indexing the thresholds for inflation, raising the taxable percentage above 85%, or eliminating the tax entirely. As of 2026, no changes have been enacted. The thresholds have remained unchanged since 1993, meaning inflation automatically pushes more retirees into taxable territory each year.

The single most powerful strategy is Roth conversions during early retirement years before claiming Social Security. Modigliani sculpture heads Phillips’s Upcoming York evening sale at $44.6m

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees).
  • Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.
  • Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

Sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

In a recent development, on the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

According to recent reports, the piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s Latest York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

The evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

Rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

The night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

Sources indicate that and while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

#68822. Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year unveiled

Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year unveiled

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.
  • The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.
  • It has been revealed that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.

The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.

It has been revealed that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau. It was also named residential interior (small) project of the year.

“This was probably the boldest and most well-executed project we saw,” stated the judges.

“They kept everything that was already there and made a much more interesting place,” adding that, “it’s very well-thought-out in terms of how space has been used.”.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners, including a restaurant that features “direct and unrefined” materials to create tactile interior in Canada, a pink stepped-facade-fronted commercial building and interiors in Mexico and a boutique that recalls a traditional yurt in Kazakhstan.

A boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture and a warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning interiors projects below:.

Interiors project of the year and residential interior (small) of the year: La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The Spanish practice renovated the home in Mataro, Spain, which belonged to a sailor in the 19th century, updating its interiors to suit the lifestyle of his descendant, who lives there now.

There was no discussion – this was the winner.

Recent findings suggest that the project saw the renovation of three spaces: the entrance hall, the dining room and the living area. The judges praised the project’s bold approach, noting there was no deliberation over its winning credentials: “There was no discussion – this was the winner.”.

“It’s super unusual,” they continued, “and we liked to see an intervention in a very historical space where they decided to not play it safe.”.

Residential interior (large) of the year: Garden Home by Gisbert Pöppler.

Local studio Gisbert Pöppler won residential interior (large) of the year for its renovation of a 1920s villa in Ruhr, Germany.

For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior.

The interior design features a bold colour scheme and artisanal details that reflect its association with the Deutscher Werkbund movement, which caught the judges’ eyes.

“For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior,” they stated.

“It has character and doesn’t play it safe,” they continued.

Restaurant interior of the year: Jeju by &Daughters.

Canadian studio &Daughters won restaurant interior of the year for Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver, Canada.

This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element.

A rich material palette of basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood characterises the restaurant interior, which nods to traditional touches in its contemporary design.

Sources indicate that “This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element,” the master jury noted. “It’s contemporary and still a bit traditional. There’s also a cultural influence that’s being used well and isn’t just there for decoration.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Bar and cafe interior of the year: Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design.

Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design in Xi’an, China, won bar and cafe interior of the year, sponsored by Programa.

There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.

Located inside the Beilin Museum, the cafe’s interior aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty and used a minimal intervention renovation strategy with every fresh addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

“This project is upcoming and modern, but still connected to the past,” the judges said.

“There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.”.

“The architect has taken symbolic elements and simplified them, which makes it feel quite fresh.”.

Hotel and short-stay interior of the year: Moon Gang by YSG Studio.

Australian studio YSG won hotel and short-stay interior of the year for its conversion of a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali, Indonesia.

There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit.

Focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture, Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

YSG was influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit,” commended the master jury.

Workplace interior (small) of the year: Rosadoce by Reims 502.

Rosadoce by Reims 502 in Querétaro, Mexico won workplace interior (small) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior.

Featuring a stepped facade, the commercial building’s pink characterises the warm feel of the interior, being used throughout the workplace with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone.

“This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior,” noted the master jury.

“We like how they connected the interior and exterior design,” they continued, “it’s an adaptable and very sophisticated design.”.

Workplace interior (large) of the year: Not A Hotel Office by Not A Hotel.

Not a Hotel’s own office in Tokyo, Japan won workplace interior (large) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic.

The Japanese hospitality tech giant’s in-house architecture team turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace featuring a brutalist design divided by glass partitions and a spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

“We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic,” mentioned the judges.

“It really makes coming to the office feel like a dip back into the culture.”.

Retail interior (small) of the year: Gunia Project Showroom by Temp Project.

Local studio Temp Project won retail interior (small) of the year for its lifestyle store in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The mix between the old and new is very interesting.

Modern materials, including mirrors and tiled surfaces, were used to complement the building’s original ornate interior for brand Gunia Project, which occupies the ground floor of a late 19th-century building located on a historic street near Kyiv’s Golden Gate.

“The mix between the old and fresh is very interesting,” stated the judges.

“It must have been a constraining space to work in,” they observed, “but the end result feels very carefully edited and sophisticated.”.

Retail interior (large) of the year: Messa House by Up2date.

Up2date Architects won retail interior (large) of the year for the minimalist Messa House store in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect.

Commissioned for womenswear brand Messa, the 350-square-metre store was designed to reimagine the form of a Kazakh yurt, with breakout areas and an on-site cafe.

“Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect,” praised the master jury.

The judges also commended “the contrast between the glossy tiles, wall and furniture”.

“It’s like a small architectural world inside the space,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Leisure and wellness interior of the year: Unravel by Atelier Write.

Japanese studio Atelier Write won the leisure and wellness interior of the year for its hair salon project in Tokyo, Japan.

This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there.

Named Unravel, the project transformed a warehouse with statement features such as suspending mirrors, shelves and curtains from a series of industrial rails that allow the entire space to be reconfigured.

“This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there,” mentioned the judges.

“It’s an innovative, moveable space and the movement has purpose; it’s not just a gimmick.”.

Exhibition design (interior) of the year: Life Behind the Walls by B² Architecture.

B2 Architecture won exhibition design (interior) of the year for its Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, Czech Republic.

They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way.

Using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea, the 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

“In this project, the colours black, white and red are used really well in a graphical way,” noted the master jury.

The judges also noted its material sensitivity, noting how surprising “the designers use soft materials to create emotions,” adding that “there’s a contrast between the technology and the use of textiles”.

“They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way,” they added.

Kitchen interior of the year: Pine Island Cottage by Thom Fougere Studio & Bureau Tempo.

Canadian studios Bureau Tempo and Thom Fougere won kitchen interior of the year for Pine Island Cottage in Ontario, Canada.

You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.

The getaway retreat’s materials are informed by the rocky surroundings of the host island in Ontario’s Georgian Bay.

“This kitchen is very functional and well laid out, but it’s also super beautiful and we like that they used local materials,” remarked the master jury.

“You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.”.

Bathroom interior of the year: Lumeah by Pepper & Well.

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well won bathroom interior of the year for Lumeah in Macedon, Australia.

We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass.

The studio took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing the fresh en-suite within one of the most intact examples of residential work by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

“We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass,” remarked the judges.

“The studio did a good job of creating a contemporary interior in a historic building, and we enjoyed how the bathroom feels like it continues out into the garden.”.

Sustainable interior of the year: Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo Design Studio.

Chinese studio RooMoo won sustainable interior of the year for Cloudhaus Hotel in Chongqing, China.

This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins were repurposed for the 24-room retreat for its renovation, which the judges noted for being well-documented.

“This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done,” the master jury stated.

“They took a dark, concrete space and turned it into a warm interior through the use of wood, while keeping a lot of the existing materials,” they continued.

Sources indicate that dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#68815. Mutabor Unveils the Voith brand identity

Mutabor Unveils the Voith brand identity

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.
  • It has been revealed that the whole system starts with a single chevron.
  • According to recent reports, the custom typeface carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

It has been revealed that the whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking new ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

According to recent reports, the custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it demonstrates in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

Sources indicate that one frame shows the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

The system proves itself where the company actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Industry observers note that some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

See the full Voith case study from Mutabor.

#68814. Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Newly introduced York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Newly introduced York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

Thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

In a recent development, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

Industry observers note that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Upcoming York in May 1986 for $1m.

It has been revealed that gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

Sources indicate that A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s Fresh York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

Impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s New York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

In a recent development, french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s Upcoming York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Substantial name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively major price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Sources indicate that picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

Sources indicate that the Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s Upcoming York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in Latest York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Sources indicate that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, Newly introduced Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

It hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s New York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

In a recent development, “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

#68812. Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2793 w)
